did_you_know.text: Did you know? When Moses is called “God to Pharaoh,” it does not mean that he is a god, but that he is given authority to speak in God’s name; Aaron serves as his prophet and spokesman.
Did you know? Moses and Aaron are described as very old leaders here: Moses is eighty and Aaron is eighty-three. The story thus suggests that leadership is not reserved for the young.
Did you know? The Hebrew word tannin can refer to a large snake or a great water creature, so “serpent” is not its only possible translation.
Did you know? The Egyptian sorcerers were court specialists connected with religious knowledge, rituals, and written learning; they were not merely “magicians” in the modern sense.
Did you know? The Nile was central to Egypt’s water supply, farming, and transportation, so meeting Pharaoh beside it has symbolic as well as political significance.
Did you know? Turning the Nile’s water into blood strikes at Egypt’s main source of life. The plague is therefore presented not only as a disaster, but also as a challenge to Egyptian power.
Did you know? The verse lists several kinds of water sources—rivers, canals, ponds, and reservoirs—to portray a widespread impact on Egypt’s entire water system.

Did you know? The Egyptian sorcerers imitate the sign, but they do not solve the water shortage. Their imitation gives Pharaoh an excuse to persist in refusing rather than acknowledge the plague’s power.
Did you know? When the Nile’s water becomes undrinkable, the Egyptians must dig near it to find water. The scene shows how quickly a major crisis changes daily life.
Did you know? The first plague is not presented as a momentary event: the verse explicitly says that the situation lasted seven days, emphasizing the crisis’s severity.
